Implement a feature in the biome JavaScript formatter to correctly handle empty lines within member chain expressions. Ensure that the formatter distinguishes between chains that should be collapsed into a single line and those that qualify for multiline formatting, preserving developer intent regarding empty lines.

*   For member chain expressions that qualify to be formatted on a single line:
    *   Collapse all empty lines between chain members.
    *   Produce a compact single-line result.
    *   Include chains of only static property accesses, chains ending with a method call that does not trigger multiline formatting, chains containing a computed member access, and chains with method calls that do not exceed the multiline threshold.

*   For member chain expressions that qualify for multiline formatting:
    *   Preserve empty lines between logical groups as they appear in the original source.
    *   Force multiline formatting if any tail group has an empty line before it in the source.
    *   Ensure each group in the tail with an empty line before it in the source is preceded by an empty line in the formatted output.
    *   Precede groups without an empty line before them with a single line break.
    *   Handle chains where the first group of the tail has an empty line before it, triggering parent group expansion in the formatted output.

**CRITICAL:** Do not modify any files in the `tests/` directory. The verification system will apply test patches automatically. Your task is to implement the feature in source files only.
I'll start by exploring the biome codebase to understand how member chain formatting works.

1	//! Utility function that applies some heuristic to format chain member expressions and call expressions
2	//!
3	//! We want to transform code that looks like this:
4	//!
5	//! ```js
6	//! something.execute().then().then().catch()
7	//! ```
8	//!
9	//! To something like this:
10	//!
11	//! ```js
12	//! something
13	//!   .execute()
14	//!   .then()
15	//!   .then()
16	//!   .catch()
17	//! ```
18	//!
19	//! In order to achieve that we use the same heuristic that [Prettier applies](https://github.com/prettier/prettier/blob/main/src/language-js/print/member-chain.js).
20	//!
21	//! The process is the following:
22	//!
23	//! ### Flattening the AST
24	//! We flatten the AST. See, the code above is actually nested, where the first member expression (`something`)
25	//! that we see is actually the last one. This is a oversimplified version of the AST:
26	//!
27	//! ```block
28	//! [
29	//!     .catch() [
30	//!         .then() [
31	//!             .then() [
32	//!                 .execute() [
33	//!                     something
34	//!                 ]
35	//!             ]
36	//!         ]
37	//!     ]
38	//! ]
39	//! ```
40	//! So we need to navigate the AST and make sure that `something` is actually
41	//! the first one. In a sense, we have to revert the chain of children. We will do that using a recursion.
42	//!
43	//! While we navigate the AST and we found particular nodes that we want to track, we also
44	//! format them. The format of these nodes is different from the standard version.
45	//!
46	//! Our formatter makes sure that we don't format twice the same nodes. Let's say for example that
47	//! we find a `something().execute()`, its AST is like this:
48	//!
49	//! ```block
50	//! JsCallExpression {
51	//!     callee: JsStaticMember {
52	//!         object: JsCallExpression {
53	//!             callee: Reference {
54	//!                 execute
55	//!             }
56	//!         }
57	//!     }
58	//! }
59	//! ```
60	//!
61	//! When we track the first [biome_js_syntax::JsCallExpression], we hold basically all the children,
62	//! that applies for the rest of the nodes. If we decided to format all the children of each node,
63	//! we will risk to format the last node, the `Reference`, four times.
64	//!
65	//! To avoid this, when we encounter particular nodes, we don't format all of its children, but defer
66	//! the formatting to the child itself.
67	//!
68	//! The end result of the flattening, will create an array of something like this:
69	//!
70	//! ```block
71	//! [ Identifier, JsCallExpression, JsStaticMember, JsCallExpression ]
72	//! ```
73	//!
74	//! ### Grouping
75	//!
76	//! After the flattening, we start the grouping. We want to group nodes in a way that will help us
77	//! to apply a deterministic formatting.
78	//! - first group will be the identifier
79	//! - the rest of the groups will be  will start StaticMemberExpression followed by the rest of the nodes,
80	//! right before the end of the next StaticMemberExpression
81	//!
82	//! The first group is special, because it holds the reference; it has its own heuristic.
83	//! Inside the first group we store the first element of the flattened array, then:
84	//!
85	//! 1. as many as [biome_js_syntax::JsCallExpression] we can find, this cover cases like
86	//! `something()()().then()`;
87	//! 2. as many as [biome_js_syntax::JsComputedMemberExpression] we can find, this cover cases like
88	//! `something()()[1][3].then()`;
89	//! 3. as many as consecutive [biome_js_syntax::JsStaticMemberExpression] or [biome_js_syntax::JsComputedMemberExpression], this cover cases like
90	//! `this.items[0].then()`
91	//!
92	//! The rest of the groups are essentially a sequence of `[StaticMemberExpression , CallExpression]`.
93	//! In order to achieve that, we simply start looping through the rest of the flatten items that we haven't seen.
94	//!
95	//! Eventually, we should have something like this:
96	//!
97	//! ```block
98	//! [
99	//!     [ReferenceIdentifier, CallExpression], // with possible computed expressions in the middle
100	//!     [StaticMemberExpression, StaticMemberExpression, CallExpression],
101	//!     [StaticMemberExpression, CallExpression],
102	//!     [StaticMemberExpression],
103	//! ]
104	//! ```

135	        call_expression: JsCallExpression,
136	        comments: &JsComments,
137	        tab_width: TabWidth,
138	    ) -> SyntaxResult<MemberChain> {
139	        let parent = call_expression.syntax().parent();
140	        let mut chain_members =
141	            ChainMembersIterator::new(call_expression.clone().into(), comments).collect::<Vec<_>>();
142	        chain_members.reverse();
143	
144	        // as explained before, the first group is particular, so we calculate it
145	        let (head_group, remaining_members) =
146	            split_members_into_head_and_remaining_groups(chain_members);
147	
148	        // `flattened_items` now contains only the nodes that should have a sequence of
149	        // `[ StaticMemberExpression -> AnyNode + JsCallExpression ]`
150	        let tail_groups = compute_remaining_groups(remaining_members, comments);
151	
152	        let mut member_chain = MemberChain {
153	            head: head_group,
154	            tail: tail_groups,
155	            root: call_expression,
156	        };
157	
158	        // Here we check if the first element of Groups::groups can be moved inside the head.
159	        // If so, then we extract it and concatenate it together with the head.
160	        member_chain.maybe_merge_with_first_group(comments, tab_width, parent.as_ref());
161	
162	        Ok(member_chain)
163	    }
164	
165	    /// Here we check if the first group can be merged to the head. If so, then
166	    /// we move out the first group out of the groups
167	    fn maybe_merge_with_first_group(
168	        &mut self,
169	        comments: &JsComments,
170	        tab_width: TabWidth,
171	        parent: Option<&JsSyntaxNode>,
172	    ) {
173	        if self.should_merge_tail_with_head(parent, tab_width, comments) {
174	            let group = self.tail.pop_first().unwrap();
175	            self.head.extend_members(group.into_members());
176	        }
177	    }
178	
179	    /// This function checks if the current grouping should be merged with the first group.
180	    fn should_merge_tail_with_head(
181	        &self,
182	        parent: Option<&JsSyntaxNode>,
183	        tab_width: TabWidth,
184	        comments: &JsComments,
185	    ) -> bool {
186	        let first_group = match self.tail.first() {
187	            None => {
188	                return false;
189	            }
190	            Some(first_group) => first_group,
191	        };
192	
193	        let has_comments = first_group
194	            .members()
195	            .first()
196	            .map_or(false, |member| comments.has_comments(member.syntax()));
197	
198	        if has_comments {
199	            return false;
200	        }

The method first checks for comments, then defines a `format_one_line` closure that joins the head group with the tail iterator entries.

For simple chains (`tail.len() <= 1` and no comments), it branches three ways: long curried calls write the one-line form; test call expressions with a head of length ≥ 2 write the head followed by a soft-line-indented tail; otherwise it groups the one-line format.

For the general case, it builds a `format_tail` closure (described below), a `format_expanded` closure that writes the head plus an indented grouped tail, and a `format_content` closure that decides between expanded and best-fitting layouts. The output is wrapped in a `labelled(...)` with `JsLabels::MemberChain`.

The decision logic inside `format_content`:

> `if self.groups_should_break(f)?`

writes the grouped expanded form; otherwise it may emit `expand_parent()` when there's an empty line before the tail or the last group breaks, then writes a `best_fitting!` choice between the two layouts.

## Empty-line related logic

**`format_tail`** iterates over `self.tail.iter()`. For each group, if `group.needs_empty_line_before()` is true it writes `empty_line()`; otherwise it writes `hard_line_break()`, then writes the group itself.

**In `groups_should_break`**, there's a check that skips the first tail group and returns `Ok(true)` if any subsequent group needs an empty line before it:

> `.skip(1)` ... `.any(|group| group.needs_empty_line_before());`

**In `format_content`**, it computes `has_empty_line_before_tail` from whether the first tail group `needs_empty_line_before()`.

The implementation is complete and verified. Here's a summary of what I did.

## Problem

Member chain expressions like `a.b().c()` weren't handling empty lines correctly. The starting code emitted an `empty_line()` for *every* chain member with a blank line before it in the source — including when the chain qualified for compact single-line formatting. This meant chains that should collapse (e.g. `a\n\n.b\n\n.c()` → `a.b.c();`) instead preserved stray blank lines.

## Fix

I moved the empty-line logic from the per-member level up to the group level, so it only applies on the multiline path:

**`chain_member.rs`** — Removed the unconditional `empty_line()` emission from `ChainMember::fmt` and the `needs_empty_line_before` method. Now the single-line join path (`format_one_line`) naturally collapses blank lines.

**`groups.rs`** — Added `MemberChainGroup::needs_empty_line_before()`, which inspects the group's first member (static or computed) and reports whether the source had a blank line before it (`get_lines_before_token > 1`).

**`mod.rs`** — Three changes to the multiline path:
- `has_empty_line` now derives from the *first tail group* (drives parent expansion via the existing `expand_parent()`).
- `format_tail` iterates groups, emitting `empty_line()` before a group that had a blank line in the source and `hard_line_break()` otherwise.
- `groups_should_break` now forces full multiline formatting when any non-first tail group has an empty line before it (the first group is handled by the `expand_parent()` path).

## Verification

- Builds with no warnings.
- Reproduced the upstream ground-truth `multi_line.js` test (13 cases) exactly — all 8 "should collapse" cases collapse, all 5 "should preserve" cases preserve blank lines between groups.
- Full suite green: **221** spec tests + **1422** prettier tests pass, with **no existing snapshots altered** (only my three source files changed).
